title: Instructed Thoughts Under the Lens
takeaway: Three interactive examples show that when the model is told to hold something in mind — a concept, a mental calculation, a silent count — that content rises to the top of J-lens readouts at output tokens whose visible text is unrelated, while none of it appears in what the model actually writes. This is the paper's qualitative demonstration that workspace contents respond to instruction alone.
walkthrough:
This item is a live widget rather than a static plot. It presents three prompt transcripts, each with one token boxed. Hovering on a layer reveals the top [[jacobian-lens]] readout tokens at that layer for the boxed position. The model is [[claude-model-family]] Sonnet 4.5.

The first two examples use the [[hold-in-mind-copy-task]]: an instruction says what to think about, and the model then copies the unrelated sentence "The old painting hung crookedly on the wall". The lens is read at the token "ook" inside "crookedly", where the surface text carries nothing about the instruction. If a concept shows up there, the instruction put it there.

In the first example the instruction is to "concentrate on citrus fruits". Across a range of layers the top lens token is orange, with lemon sometimes among the top entries. At intermediate layers the readout also carries fruit, thoughts, imagine, thinking, focused, and imagery — [[metacognitive-representations]] describing the side task in the abstract. The readouts thus hold both the imagined content and a representation of the act of imagining it. In the final layers the readout switches to "edly", the next output token; the paper reads this as the workspace ending a few layers before the [[motor-layers]] that select the output.

In the second example the instruction is to focus on evaluating $3^2 - 2$. Three squared is nine. Nine minus two is seven. The lens at the same "ook" position tracks exactly this: arithmetic and math at early layers, the intermediate nine at later layers, then seven alongside answer and equals.

The third example is the [[character-counting-task]]: the model silently counts the characters in each line of a passage. At the newline after a 40-character line, readouts move from lines, sentence, and length to forty, with 39, 41, 43, fifty, and thirty nearby.

None of this processing is visible in the model's output distribution. That is the point: the [[j-space]] is subject to [[directed-modulation]]. These are single illustrative trials; the systematic comparison of [[instruction-conditions]] — where a no-instruction baseline sits near zero, "think about X" loads the target on a substantial fraction of trials, and "ignore X" lands in between — is quantified in the next figure.

terms.definition: The lens's basic read operation: the residual-stream activation at a layer is mapped through an averaged Jacobian and the unembedding, producing a ranked list of vocabulary tokens. The widget shows the top of that list per layer.
The single token position in each transcript at which the lens is read; in the copying examples it is "ook" inside "crookedly", in the counting example a newline.
One depth of the model's residual stream; hovering a layer in the widget reveals the top readout tokens at that depth for the boxed position.
The production Claude model these three examples are run on, the mid-size tier of the family used throughout the paper.
The protocol behind the first two examples: an instruction says what to hold in mind, the model copies an unrelated sentence, and the lens is read at the copied tokens.
The instruction in the first example; the concept it names, not the copied sentence, is what the lens then finds.
The token inside "crookedly" at which the lens is read in the first two examples; its surface text is unrelated to the instructed content.
The instructed citrus content surfacing in the readout: orange is the top lens token across a range of layers, and lemon sometimes appears among the top entries.

terms.term: fruit, thoughts, imagine, thinking, focused, imagery
terms.definition: Intermediate-layer readout tokens that describe the side task in the abstract — the act of imagining, alongside the imagined content itself.
The final token of "crookedly", the model's next output token; the readout switches to it in the last few layers, marking where the workspace gives way to output selection.
Early-layer readout tokens in the second example, naming the kind of task before any result exists.
The intermediate value $3^2 = 9$, appearing in the readout at later layers than the task description.
The final result $9 - 2 = 7$ and its framing, appearing at even later layers than the intermediate.
The third example's protocol: the model silently tracks the number of characters in each line of a multi-line passage, and the lens is read at a newline token.
Early-layer readout tokens at the newline, describing the counting task before the count itself appears.
The correct character count of the second line, surfacing in intermediate-layer readouts at the newline that ends it.
The workspace property this figure illustrates: the model can deliberately load a concept into workspace representations when instructed, independent of its outputs.

The compared instruction types in the surrounding experiments: a focus instruction, an ignore instruction, and a no-instruction baseline (with mention and don't-think variants in the appendix). The figure's examples are all of the focus kind.
The set of activation-space points expressible as sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the region these readouts inspect, and the paper's workspace candidate.

numbers.meaning: The number of example prompts in the widget: a held concept, a mental calculation, and a silent count — one per task family later quantified systematically.
The expression the model is told to evaluate mentally in the second example while copying an unrelated sentence; chosen so that it has a distinct intermediate and answer.
The intermediate value of the mental calculation, $3^2$; it appears in the lens readout at later layers than the abstract task tokens and earlier layers than the answer.
The answer to the mental calculation, $9 - 2$; it reaches the readout at even later layers, so the lens shows the computation unfolding across depth.
The character count of the second line in the counting example; forty appears in intermediate-layer readouts at the newline ending that line.
Nearby number candidates present in the readout alongside forty — the count is represented with some spread rather than as a single exact token.
Where the readout switches from held content to the predicted next token ("edly"); the paper's evidence elsewhere is that the workspace ends a few layers before the model's last layer.
